props.html: Last Consulate is the solo project of one multi-instrumentalist, built on upright bass, electric bass, guitar and downtempo electronics.

The improvising is jazz. The production is early-2000s downtempo electronica, the slow and hazy end of it, instrumental and warm, and mixed so that what was played and what was sampled are hard to tell apart.
Upright bass is the lead instrument. Under it sit slow hip-hop drums, extended jazz harmony, tape-worn keys and delayed guitars, and the improvised bass line is usually the melody.

It is built for arrival, cocktails and dinner, played at a volume guests can talk across, with the feel of a late jazz set or a hotel lobby. The loops hold the tempo in the slow band all evening, so the music never drifts up as the venue fills. It sounds like a record playing in a very good hotel, until somebody notices the bass line is being played live.

items.a: Original instrumental music: upright bass and guitar out front over downtempo electronics, with jazz improvisation on top. It sounds closer to an early-2000s downtempo record than to a jazz set, and it's booked through Signet Artists in Denver.
It plays arrival, cocktails and dinner at about the level of the conversation, so your guests talk across it the whole time, and the bass lines are improvised live on the night.

items.q: Does it play covers or take requests?
items.a: No. Everything is original and instrumental, with no singer, which is part of why a client dinner books it: there's nothing on the night for the host to manage.

One musician and one rig. It sets up in about 6 by 4 feet on one dedicated 20-amp circuit, takes 45 minutes to set up, and plays through its own small sound system or the venue's house system, whichever the space wants.

items.q: Can it carry a whole evening?
items.a: Arrival through dinner, yes. When the night wants a dance floor afterward, a band or the DJ takes over on the same contract and the same sound system, so Last Consulate is the first half of one booking.
